articles.title: From about 1950 to 1964, a Washington janitor spent nights in a rented garage assembling a 180-piece throne from foil, cardboard, old furniture and light bulbs; it now fills a Smithsonian gallery
articles.summary: Discover the story of James Hampton, a Washington janitor who created an extraordinary 180-piece religious installation from discarded materials, now featured in the Smithsonian American Art Museum.
articles.body: For about 14 years, James Hampton worked in a rented carriage house in Washington, D.C., assembling a religious installation out of discarded objects and inexpensive materials. The self-taught artist built around 180 separate components for The Throne of the Third Heaven of the Nations’ Millennium General Assembly, a work he based on religious visions and his faith in Christ’s return.Hampton worked on the project while working as a janitor for the General Services Administration. Rather than using conventional sculptural materials, he transformed old furniture, cardboard, plastic, jelly jars and discarded light bulbs to create a highly ordered installation. Gold and silver foil, purple paper and other reflective materials covered many of the surfaces, giving the objects a bright appearance despite their humble origins. The Smithsonian American Art Museum now holds the work, which is listed as a mixed-media sculpture and assemblage dating from about 1950 to 1964.A religious vision realised from discarded objects The installation is centred on a throne surrounded by rows of crowns, altars, lecterns, tablets and other objects. Hampton arranged the components in parallel rows across two levels, to create a pronounced symmetry, with the central throne acting as the focal point, while the two sides consist of biblical references. The museum identified the left side with the Old Testament and Moses, while the right side alluded to the New Testament and Jesus. Hampton's use of the term “third heaven” came from scripture describing the “heaven of heavens” as being the realm of God.At the centre is the phrase “FEAR NOT”, taken from the book of Revelation, while other components are marked with biblical references and inscriptions and Hampton’s own handwritten labels for individual sections, according to the Smithsonian American Art Museum. His religious ideas extended beyond the objects into a notebook called “The Book of the 7 Dispensation” which is written largely in an invented or asemic script that remains difficult to interpret, according to the Smithsonian American Art Museum.Hampton referred to himself as “ST JAMES”, and much akin to the Bible, its pages are organised in numbered chapters, according to Smithsonian Magazine. The museum presentation also includes a chalkboard showing sketches or working plans, offering a glimpse into how Hampton developed his ideas. Beyond its biblical imagery, the museum describes the work as a combination of Christianity with African-American spiritual practices rife with themes of deliverance and freedom.From a hidden garage to the Smithsonian Hampton did not live to see his work exhibited at the museum and died from cancer in 1964, leaving the installation unfinished. After his death, his landlord, Myer Wertlieb, went to the rented garage to collect overdue rent and discovered the enormous collection of work assembled there. Wertlieb initially struggled to find someone willing to take the work until the installation eventually came to the attention of sculptor Ed Kelly, who contacted an art collector. This set off a chain of contacts that brought it to Harry Lowe, then an exhibitions and design official at the National Collection of Fine Arts.Lowe later recalled to the Washington Post entering the garage as being “like opening Tut’s tomb”. He paid Hampton’s outstanding rent and arranged for the entire assembly to be acquired by the museum, and a selection from its central section was first exhibited in 1971. Since then, the work has become one of the most recognised examples of American visionary art, and its significance also prompted the continuation of conservation work. Museum staff have catalogued, cleaned, examined, photographed, scanned and restored its individual components, allowing the installation to be studied piece by piece.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India on Saturday termed the United Nations Human Rights Commission's concern over the mass detention of protesters in Delhi as \"misplaced\" and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India on Saturday termed the United Nations Human Rights Commission's concern over the mass detention of protesters in Delhi as "misplaced" and said the right to peaceful assembly is guaranteed by the country's Constitution.In a social media post on X, India at UN said the remarks by the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) amounted to "unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India"."We have seen the OHCHR’s remarks about today’s events in New Delhi. India is the world’s largest democracy, where the right to peaceful assembly is guaranteed by our Constitution and safeguarded by robust institutions, an independent judiciary, and a free media," it said."As in every democracy, Indian citizens exercise this right subject to reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order. The authorities, for their part, act in accordance with the law, and our courts remain available to all for redressal of any grievances. The OHCHR’s concerns are therefore misplaced and constitute an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India," it added.It also advised the international body to "devote comparable attention" to large-scale protests in different parts of the world."In this context, OHCHR would also do well to devote comparable attention to large-scale protests elsewhere, consistent with its mandate of impartiality and non-selectivity," it said.This comes after the OHCHR raised concerns over mass detentions during the Cockroach Janata Party-led protest in New Delhi against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: HC quashes Tellapur land acquisition, relief for plot owners
articles.summary: Telangana High Court quashes 2006–07 Tellapur land acquisition for township, citing vague public purpose and flawed Section 5-A inquiry; relief for plot owners.
articles.body: Hyderabad: In a significant relief to hundreds of plot owners in Tellapur, Telangana high court has quashed land acquisition proceedings initiated nearly two decades ago for a proposed township, holding that the acquisition was marred by both procedural and substantive illegality.Justice Vakiti Ramakrishna Reddy struck down the 2006 land acquisition notification and the 2007 declaration issued for acquiring lands in Tellapur, observing that the stated purpose of acquiring land for the formation or development of a township and future projects was vague and failed to provide landowners sufficient clarity to raise meaningful objections.The case relates to 92.39 acres spread across several survey numbers in Tellapur, earmarked for acquisition by the district collector on behalf of HUDA, now HMDA. The land forms part of 326.37 acres that were earlier held by the Industrial Employees Co-operative House Building Society.Allowing petitions filed by a plot owners’ association and five individuals, Justice Reddy held that while the authorities were free to initiate fresh acquisition proceedings, if necessary, they must do so strictly in accordance with the law.The petitioners argued that the land had been converted for non-agricultural use as early as 1986, laid out into plots, and had previously been excluded from acquisition in 1989 after consideration by the govt. They contended that the subsequent acquisition was essentially aimed at facilitating real estate development, pointing out that HUDA had invited tenders for township development even while objections to the acquisition were pending.The state govt and HMDA, however, maintained that planned township development constituted a valid public purpose. They argued that the term “township” was a recognised statutory expression and that completion of the acquisition process had been delayed because of interim court orders that had remained in force since 2007.The authorities also relied on subsequent statutory provisions that protected acquisition proceedings affected by court-imposed stays.Rejecting these contentions, the court noted that the same acquisition notification had already been quashed in a related Tellapur land acquisition case in Feb. It observed that the acquisition could not be held invalid for one set of similarly placed landowners while remaining valid for others covered by the same notification.The court also found fault with the Section 5-A enquiry conducted under the Land Acquisition Act, noting that the exercise had been reduced to a mere formality. articles.title: Protesters demand SIR rollback, slam police action
articles.summary: Hyderabad rally opposes SIR electoral roll revision, alleges illegal detentions en route to Delhi protest; CJP members detained in MP return, seek accountability.
articles.body: Hyderabad: A protest against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls was held in the city on Saturday evening, with protesters opposing the exercise and the alleged illegal detentions of those travelling to New Delhi to participate in a demonstration at Jantar Mantar.Organised by the Disha Students Organisation, Naujawan Bharat Sabha and Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), the rally, comprising around 100 people, passed through residential lanes as local residents watched. Protesters raised slogans such as “scrap SIR”, “arrest CEC Gyanesh Kumar”, “cancel all elections post-SIR” and “reconduct elections”.The protest was also attended by retired IAS officer and former Telangana education commission chairperson Akunuri Murali, rights activist Padmaja Sharma and economist Rathan Roy. Kriti, a resident of Himayathnagar, questioned the changes to Form 6 and the govt’s handling of the exercise. “The SIR process and analysis have come up, and the changes in Form 6 are not right. The govt has an agenda and is diverting attention from major issues such as unemployment and the NEET controversy,” she said.An IT employee who attended the rally said the protest offered people an opportunity to raise their concerns. K Suresh, a student, questioned the rationale behind the exercise. “If the SIR is meant only to remove illegal immigrants, the govt should clarify how many of the 13 crore voters are illegal immigrants. Instead, voter names have been deleted over the past year,” he said.Protestors also highlighted that the issue went beyond voting rights. “Disenfranchisement is not just about taking away the right to vote, but also the right to life and the right to exist,” said Loraine from the English and Foreign Languages University (EFLU). Her friend Nishtha recounted how a friend whose name had been deleted from the voter list had been distressed.Detainees returnEarlier in the day, the four CJP members detained at Bhopal railway station on the night of Oct 8 reached Warangal in the early hours of Saturday. Madhya Pradesh police escorted them to Warangal. “We were travelling to Delhi with a purpose, not for entertainment, but to raise our voices through peaceful democratic protest. Detaining us and other CJP supporters raises serious concerns about our democratic rights. We demand to know under what law we were detained, why we were denied clear reasons for our detention and contact with our families, and who will be held accountable,” said Rajesh Korapaka, one of the four detainees. articles.title: CM Mann flags off anti-drug bike rally from Chappar Chiri
articles.summary: Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann flags off anti-drug bike rally from Chappar Chiri, covering all 23 districts with suggestion and complaint boxes under Yudh Nashean Virudh.
articles.body: Chandigarh: Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann on Saturday flagged off a bikers’ rally from Chappar Chiri in Mohali to cover all 23 districts as part of the final phase of the state govt’s anti-drug campaign, Yudh Nashean Virudh.The rally will carry suggestion boxes for public feedback and complaint boxes for reporting drug traffickers. Mann urged young people to shun drugs and embrace education and sports, while blaming previous BJP, Akali and Congress govts for spreading drugs and diminishing Punjab’s glory.In a post on X, Mann said the fight against drugs was not just the responsibility of the govt or police but required the collective participation of Punjabis.“The ‘Yudh Nashean Virudh’ cannot be won by the govt alone and requires the united strength of every Punjabi,” he said, urging people from all walks of life to join the campaign.Mann said the rally would take the anti-drug message to villages, towns and communities across Punjab. A dedicated vehicle would accompany the bikers to collect public feedback and suggestions on the welfare and development of the state.He said the complaint box would allow people to report drug traffickers or share information about them. articles.title: Jail officer held for helping inmates get opium, phones in Ludhiana lock-up
articles.summary: Ludhiana Central Jail assistant superintendent arrested after inquiry linked him to smuggling 86g opium and mobile phones to inmates; probe ongoing.
articles.body: Ludhiana: A departmental inquiry into the seizure of 86gm of opium and four mobile phones from inmates at Ludhiana Central Jail has led to the arrest of an assistant superintendent, raising fresh concerns over the alleged involvement of prison staff in facilitating the entry of prohibited items into Punjab jails.Assistant superintendent Rishavpal Goyal was arrested by Division No. 7 police Friday after a probe conducted by jail authorities found his alleged role in helping inmates obtain contraband recovered during a surprise inspection inside the prison.Confirming the development, ASI Dinesh Kumar, incharge of Tajpur Road police post, said jail authorities had initially got a case registered against nine inmates after opium and mobile phones were seized from them. “After the seizure, the jail authorities conducted a departmental inquiry during which the involvement of assistant superintendent Rishavpal Goyal surfaced,” he said.Police said the jail administration subsequently wrote to Ludhiana police seeking action against the official. Based on the findings of the inquiry, Goyal was nominated in the FIR and taken into custody. Investigators are now probing the extent of his involvement and whether a larger network was operating inside the prison.Officials said the recovery was made during a surprise check, when four mobile phones, 86 gm of opium and empty pouches were allegedly found in the possession of inmates Sonu Chaurasia and Ajay Kumar alias Ghora. The remaining inmates allegedly helped conceal the contraband, leading to the registration of a case against all nine prisoners.The latest arrest comes at a time when prison authorities are already grappling with allegations of corruption and security breaches involving jail personnel. In Sept, additional superintendent Balvir Singh of Ludhiana Central Jail was suspended and booked for allegedly accepting money to provide preferential treatment and better accommodation to undertrials lodged in GST fraud cases.
